CHIEF COMPLAINT
Right index finger pain and swelling following motor vehicle accident.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient is a 55-year-old right-handed male who sustained a hyperextension injury to the right index finger in March 2026 during a motor vehicle accident. He was a passenger in a vehicle that was rear-ended multiple times, which caused him to be slung forward and stretch out his right index finger. The patient reports the finger felt like it went backwards and has been painful and swollen ever since the injury, approximately six months ago. He has difficulty making a fist and reports pain with daily activities including driving. Pain is sometimes severe and unbearable. He has been evaluated at Point May Orthopedics where he underwent MRI imaging and was referred to occupational therapy. The MRI showed a tear in the flexor tendon. He was initially offered a steroid injection but declined due to a prior severe reaction to dexamethasone causing tachycardia. He subsequently was told an injection might worsen the tear, creating confusion about treatment options. He reports attempting occupational therapy but experiencing increased swelling afterward. He comes today seeking a second opinion and guidance on management.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Denies diabetes and rheumatoid arthritis. Reports history of adverse reaction to methylprednisolone causing severe itching.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
No significant chronic medical conditions reported.

MEDICATIONS
Blood pressure medication (specific agent not documented).

ALLERGIES
Dexamethasone - causes tachycardia. Methylprednisolone - causes severe itching.

FAMILY HISTORY
Not documented.

SOCIAL HISTORY
Patient works as an x-ray technician. He is right-handed and depends on hand function for his occupation.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
General: Pleasant, cooperative, healthy-appearing male in no acute distress. Heart rate regular rate and rhythm with 2+ radial pulse. Right hand examination reveals no swelling or bruising in the palm over the volar surface of the index finger. Normal creases noted with slightly diminished creases over the PIP joint compared to the middle finger. Index finger rests in a 10-degree PIP-flexed position. Tenderness to palpation on dorsal aspect that improves with palmar palpation. Mild numbness noted on examination. Patient experiences pain with passive extension but less pain with other maneuvers. Patient able to bend DIP and PIP joints with effort, reporting sensation of tearing with active flexion. Able to make a fist. Collateral ligaments and extensors intact on examination.

RESULTS
X-ray of right hand (four views) today: No bony abnormalities, joint congruency maintained throughout all fingers, no soft tissue shadows of concern, no evidence of arthritis.

Prior MRI dated 4/24/2021: Focal soft tissue swelling over the right index MCP joint, partial-thickness tear of the right flexor digitorum superficialis (FDS) tendon, fluid consistent with tenosynovitis around the FDP and FDS tendons, radial and ulnar collateral ligaments of the index MCP joint intact, MCP joint capsule intact, extensor tendons intact.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Post-traumatic severe stenosing tenosynovitis of the right index finger with partial-thickness tear of the right flexor digitorum superficialis tendon. The FDS is the less functionally significant of the two flexor tendons; the flexor digitorum profundus (FDP) which extends to the fingertip is intact. Collateral ligaments and extensors are intact.

Plan:
1. Steroid injection: Attempted injection of 1 cc betamethasone (Celestone) with 0.5 cc lidocaine. First attempt resulted in dramatic painful reaction with patient hand withdrawal and concern for needle stick; needle was withdrawn. Second attempt successful with minor bleeding from small palmar vein controlled with band-aid. Patient reassured multiple times that no harm was done to the finger.
2. Pain management: Ice this evening and ibuprofen as needed.
3. Rehabilitation: Outpatient occupational/physical therapy once weekly for six weeks with goals of full active and passive range of motion and no restrictions. Patient instructed that active movement and stretching are essential for recovery; splinting immobilizes and is counterproductive. Emphasized that patient cannot break bone or tear the remaining intact structures with appropriate exercise, and that movement will help reduce stiffness and scar tissue.
4. Activity: Safe to drive.
5. Follow-up: Patient reassured that pain and function should begin improving in 3-5 days with continued improvement over the following weeks. May require repeat steroid injection if needed. Discussed that the goal is to decrease inflammation and pain to allow therapeutic movement, which the patient must perform for the stiffness component.
